role: Turn a lesson request into a complete, zero-assumption learning sequence that anyone can start and finish with no background knowledge.
method: Write the objectives first, as things a learner can do or explain, and plan a post-check item for each.

Decompose every concept by asking 'what must someone already understand to follow this?' until the answer is everyday experience. Each answer becomes an assumed everyday idea, an earlier lesson, or a detour.
Lay out the sequence stage by stage in the lesson grammar order. In every step, give the learner something to do before telling them anything.
Name an idea only after the learner has met it. Record each new term in termsIntroduced at the step where it is first used, and give it a glossary definition in plain words.
Write every calculation with all its steps. Put mathematics beyond the core path in deeper layers.
Plan for the misconceptions in the reference list that touch this concept: where each is surfaced and how it is corrected.
Read the whole sequence as a class 8 learner who reads slowly, has never seen the platform and is unsure about fractions. Fix every place they would stop.

criteria.name: Zero-assumption decomposition
criteria.description: Every concept is decomposed until it rests on everyday experience; each prerequisite is assumed-everyday, a prior lesson, or a detour with an outline.

levels.4: Every prerequisite, including numeracy and vocabulary, is found and handled; detours are short, return the learner, and none is missing.
levels.3: All conceptual prerequisites are handled; at most one minor numeracy or vocabulary assumption is left implicit.
levels.2: One real prerequisite is assumed without a detour, or a detour has no outline.
levels.1: Several prerequisites are assumed; detours are named but not designed.

criteria.name: Experience before naming
criteria.description: Learners meet each idea through an act before it is named or explained.

levels.4: Every key idea is experienced first and named after; terms are defined at first use in plain words.
levels.3: Most ideas are experienced first; one is named before it is met but defined on the spot.
levels.2: About half the ideas are told before they are experienced.
levels.1: The sequence mostly explains, then asks the learner to apply.

criteria.name: Every step shown
criteria.description: Every calculation and every 'why' is answered in the sequence; mathematics beyond the core sits in deeper layers with its own scaffolding.

levels.4: All working is shown; deeper layers carry the maths with scaffolding; nothing asks the learner to take a number on trust.
levels.3: Working is shown everywhere on the core path; a deeper layer skips one step.
levels.2: One core calculation or 'why' is left unexplained.

criteria.name: Checks measure the objectives
criteria.description: Pre-check and post-check items each map to an objective, test understanding rather than recall of wording, and include at least one transfer item.

levels.4: Every objective has at least one post-check item; items test understanding in new situations; distractors come from real misconceptions.
levels.3: Every objective is covered; one item tests recall of wording rather than understanding.
levels.2: One objective has no post-check item, or items mostly test recall.
levels.1: Checks exist but do not map to the objectives.

criteria.name: Misconceptions surfaced and corrected
criteria.description: Relevant misconceptions from the reference list are designed into the sequence: surfaced by a prediction or task, then corrected by evidence.

levels.4: Each relevant misconception is surfaced by the learner's own prediction and corrected by what they see.
levels.3: Relevant misconceptions are addressed, one only by telling.
levels.2: Misconceptions are mentioned but not designed for.
levels.1: A relevant misconception is reinforced by the wording.

criteria.name: One idea at a time, at the reading level
criteria.description: Each step introduces at most one new idea; sentences are short and in plain words for the audience's reading level; no banned phrases.

levels.4: Every step carries one idea; text would read comfortably for a class 8 learner in a second language.
levels.3: One step carries two new ideas, or a few sentences are long.
levels.2: Several overloaded steps or dense text.

text.description: What the learner can do or explain afterwards.
